newsitem.title: USA: Clinton said likely to veto some U.S. budget items.
newsitem.headline: Clinton said likely to veto some U.S. budget items.

text.p: President Bill Clinton is likely on Monday to use his new line-item veto power to eliminate certain provisions of two recently enacted laws that set the U.S. budget, senior White House aides said.

Clinton's actions would make history because for more than 100 years U.S. presidents have sought to be able to apply vetoes to specific provisions without having to block entire bills from becoming law.

Clinton's aides gave no details, but the New York Times in its Monday editions said Clinton will veto a change in the Medicaid programme and may block a tax-deferral plan for the sale of a food-processing plant.
The Times said a particular change in the Medicaid programme that the Clinton administration considers flawed policy is among likely candidates to be killed.

The newspaper also said a provision worth an estimated $84 million over five years that would allow the deferral of taxes for the sale by a Texas company of a sugar-beet processing plant to a farmers' cooperative will be cut.

On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and White House Senior Adviser Rahm Emanuel declined to say exactly what provisions Clinton would strike from the legislation, which was signed into law on Tuesday and aims to balance the budget by 2002.
"He will announce his decisions tomorrow, and he will announce that he is going to use his line-item veto. He'll use it on both the tax and the spending side," Rubin told ABC's "This Week" programme.

"He will use the line-item veto, and he'll do it tomorrow," Emanuel told "Face the Nation" on CBS. "You're going to have to tune in Monday to hear from the president. He'll tell you which ones, not me."

Emanuel suggested Clinton wanted to use the veto power to discourage the congressional backscratching that has often allowed powerful special interests to insert into legislation spending or tax provisions that benefit them.

"We are very proud of what the balanced-budget agreement did," Emanuel said. "But if there's an item that ... continues business as usual in Washington, he'll invoke the line-item authority, which he will do tomorrow."
Clinton last week said that as governor of Arkansas, where he had similar authority over state spending, he found that "once I used it a few times, I didn't need to use it very much anymore."
Sought by presidents since Ulysses S. Grant in 1876, the line-item veto allows a president to block parts of spending bills or strike down narrowly targeted tax breaks without vetoing entire bills.
Congress has often tacked special provisions onto otherwise unrelated bills, leaving the president little choice.
The line-item veto power was signed into law in 1996 and took effect on Jan. 1. Before that the president was able to veto an entire bill but not its individual components.
As with other presidential vetoes, Congress can override such action by mustering a two-thirds majority in both the House and the Senate.

There has been intense debate within the White House over whether Clinton should use the veto power on the budget bill, which aims to balance the budget by 2002, and on a companion piece that cuts taxes by a net $95 billion over five years.
Under the law he has five working days from the signing of legislation to exercise the line-item veto, giving him a deadline of midnight on Monday.

The Supreme Court in June dismissed a challenge to the line-item veto filed by six members of Congress. The court, however, did not rule on the merits of the veto, merely saying the six lacked legal standing to bring the suit.
